title: Architectural scaling tradeoffs in modular 3D bosonic quantum processors
authors: Shaojiang Zhu, Ugur Alyanak, Tanay Roy, Alessandro Reineri, Andy C. Y. Li, Taeyoon Kim, Srivatsan Chakram, Akshay Murthy, Anna Grassellino, Alexander Romanenko
abstract: We propose a modular three-dimensional bosonic quantum processor built from repeatable coupled-cavity modules linked by configurable interconnect networks. Using hardware-motivated graph-theoretic measures, we compare nearest-neighbor, hub-based, and hybrid architectures in terms of interconnect count, communication distance, resource concentration, and implementation complexity. Rather than identifying a universally optimal topology, our analysis shows how these architectures redistribute the costs of scaling, including wiring and port requirements, nonlocal communication distance, exposure to shared resources, routing bottlenecks, and scheduling overhead. Case studies of a \(3\times3\) processor and a larger hierarchical architecture further distinguish finite-size performance from asymptotic scaling. The resulting framework provides a systematic basis for evaluating modular three-dimensional bosonic processors and for identifying the device-level parameters required for quantitative hardware design.
summary: This work proposes a comprehensive graph-theoretic framework to evaluate the scaling tradeoffs in modular 3D bosonic quantum processors. By analyzing different interconnect topologies, the authors map how various hardware costs, such as wiring and communication distance, are redistributed as the system size increases. This provides a systematic guide for the hardware co-design of future large-scale quantum computers.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the architectural scaling tradeoffs for building large, modular three-dimensional (3D) bosonic quantum processors.
main_result: It develops a systematic framework showing that scaling costs (like wiring and communication distance) are redistributed across different topologies (nearest-neighbor, hub-based, hybrid), rather than having a single optimal solution.
method: The analysis uses hardware-motivated graph-theoretic measures to compare various interconnect topologies and quantify scaling costs.
model_or_system: The system is a modular QPU built from repeatable coupled-cavity modules (TBMs) connected by a structured inter-module communication graph.
key_observables: Interconnect count, communication distance ($ ar{\ell}$), resource concentration, routing bottlenecks, and scheduling overhead.
important_parameters: Local module parameters ($q, c, p, V_{cell}$), total number of modules ($N$), and specific graph metrics like edge count and module degree.
main_assumptions: Local module parameters are assumed not to scale with the total number of modules ($N$), and the analysis uses graph proxies rather than specifying coupling strengths or fidelities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical-to-architectural mapping of the TBM and compare the structural differences between nearest-neighbor, hub-based, and hybrid topologies for a small number of modules.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical TBM unit to abstracting the system as a communication graph, comparing three major interconnect strategies, and finally providing a framework for systematic cost evaluation.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial, quantitative, and systematic methodology for assessing the physical feasibility and scaling limits of large-scale quantum hardware architectures, which is vital for experimental quantum information scientists.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Physical-to-architectural mapping for a modular bosonic QPU built from TBMs. (a) Physical schematic of a TBM comprising an two-cell elliptical SRF cavity, ancillary transmon-based control and readout components, and external drive and readout interfaces. (b) Graph-level abstraction of one TBM, with local memory, control, and readout resources grouped into a module vertex. (c) Example of a hybrid communication graph containing M linear clusters of n modules.

FIG. 2. Comparison of three interconnect topologies for the same bosonic processor with 9 computational modules. (a) Nearest- neighbor grid with only local links; a representative nonlocal route requires multiple hops. (b) Hub-based architecture with a central hub connecting to all modules; the representative route uses two module-hub links. (c) hybrid row-cluster architecture that retains local row-chain connectivity while designating each row-center module as a gateway to the central hub.

FIG. 3. Architecture-level scaling comparison for the nearest-neighbor (NN), hub, and balanced hybrid interconnects. (a) Link count W, characterizing the total hardware-connectivity requirement. (b) Mean shortest-path distance ¯ℓbetween computa- tional modules, setting the baseline number of transfer steps required for communication. (c) Link-conflict scheduling depth C = χ′(G) under exclusive-endpoint activation, for which links sharing a module or routing resource cannot operate simul- taneously. (d) Normalized maximum shortest-path betweenness eB, characterizing the concentration of shortest-path traffic through intermediate vertices. (e) Normalized shared-resource burden ¯b = ∆r/N,...

FIG. 4. Topological proxy comparison for three 3 × 3 modular interconnects: nearest-neighbor (NN), global hub, and hybrid row-cluster. Panels show total number of links W, maximum graph degree ∆max, shared-hub burden ∆I, worst-case module- to-module path length ℓmax, and mean path length ¯ℓ.
